lessons.title: Best Places To Find Voiceover Jobs Right Now
objectives: Know where voice work is actually posted and what each place expects
Judge which routes are realistic from here and which are not
Sort out how you will be paid before you take a job
lessons.notes:
THE PLACES DIVIDE INTO THREE KINDS, and they want different things from you.

PAY-TO-PLAY CASTING SITES take an annual membership and send you auditions. The work can be good; the membership is charged in dollars whether or not you book anything, and beginners routinely spend a year of fees for nothing. Do not start here.

GENERAL FREELANCE MARKETPLACES let you list a service and be found. Cheaper to enter, far more crowded, and the first reviews decide everything. This is the realistic online starting point and module 6 covers setting one up properly.

DIRECT CLIENTS are the ones nobody mentions and the ones most available to you. Production houses, advertising agencies, radio stations, e-learning companies, NGOs, church media teams, and YouTube channels all commission voice work and most of them never post it anywhere public. You find them by asking.

WHAT AN AUDITION ACTUALLY IS: they post a script and a brief, you record a short piece to spec, you send it. Most of them you will not get, and that is normal rather than a verdict. Treat the first fifty as practice with a chance attached.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the parts that decide whether this works from Kenya.

WORK OUT HOW THE MONEY REACHES YOU BEFORE YOU ACCEPT ANYTHING. Most international platforms pay out through a small number of routes, and the practical ones here generally mean an intermediary account and a withdrawal fee, sometimes a currency conversion on top. On a small first job those charges can take a real bite out of the fee. Ask the platform or the client exactly how and when payment lands, agree it in writing, and factor the cost into your price rather than discovering it afterwards. A job you cannot get paid for is not a job.

BEWARE THE UNPAID TEST THAT IS ACTUALLY THE JOB. A short audition piece from a supplied script is normal and fine. Being asked to record the entire finished piece before any agreement is not an audition, it is unpaid work, and it is a known way beginners get used. A real client will agree terms first.

DO NOT COMPETE WHERE YOU ARE WEAKEST. Bidding against thousands for American-accent commercial reads with no reviews is the hardest possible opening. The local and regional work in module 1 is where a beginner here actually wins, and it pays in shillings with no withdrawal fee at all.

KEEP A SIMPLE RECORD from the first job: who, what, when, how much, paid or not. You will need it for tax eventually, and sooner than that you will need it to chase somebody who has forgotten you.
lessons.practice: Write a list of ten real potential clients you could reach without an introduction - name the actual radio stations, production houses, NGOs, churches or YouTube channels. Then pick one online platform, read its payment and withdrawal terms properly, and write down what you would actually receive on a job priced at the equivalent of KSh 5,000.

quiz.question: Which route is the hardest place for a beginner here to start?
options: Pay-to-play casting sites charging annual membership in dollars
Direct approaches to local production houses and radio stations
A general freelance marketplace listing
Recording sample work for a local NGO

quiz.question: What should you settle before accepting a first job?
options: Exactly how and when payment reaches you, and what the fees cost, agreed in writing
Which microphone the client prefers
Whether they will give you a testimonial
How many revisions they expect

lessons.title: How to Make Money Podcasting
objectives: Understand the real ways podcasts earn, and their order
Judge honestly what audience size each route needs
Find the route that works at a small, local scale
lessons.notes:
ADVERTISING IS THE LAST ROUTE, NOT THE FIRST, and most beginner podcasters have it backwards. Sponsorship is priced on downloads per episode, and the numbers required before anybody pays meaningful money are far higher than a new show will reach for a long time. Building a show in the hope of advert money is the slowest possible plan.

THE ROUTES, roughly in the order they become available to a small show:

SELLING YOUR OWN THING is first and needs the smallest audience. A podcast that reaches two hundred of exactly the right people can sell a service, a course, a consultation or a product to them. Two hundred committed listeners beats twenty thousand indifferent ones.

CLIENT WORK FROM THE SHOW comes next. The podcast is the demonstration; the income is people hiring you because of it. This is by far the commonest way podcasting pays early, and it is why the show should be about something you can be hired to do.

LISTENER SUPPORT works for a small, devoted audience, but be realistic about how few people ever pay for free content.

SPONSORSHIP comes last, and a LOCAL sponsor for a local show is far more achievable than a national brand - the sacco, the school, the shop, the clinic, who care about reaching exactly your listeners and who you can meet in person.

PRODUCING FOR OTHERS is the route almost nobody plans for and many end up taking: once you can record and edit properly, other people will pay you to do it for their show. That is a job you can hold from the first month, and module 6 covers it.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - what this looks like at a Kenyan scale.

DOWNLOAD NUMBERS THAT LOOK SMALL INTERNATIONALLY CAN BE VERY SELLABLE LOCALLY. A show with a few hundred regular listeners in one county, or in one profession, is genuinely attractive to a business trying to reach that exact group, and you can walk into their office and say so. Do not measure yourself against American download charts.

HOSTING COSTS MONEY AND DATA. Podcast hosts charge monthly in dollars once you pass a free tier, and uploading a large episode every week costs you bundle. This is a direct argument for the mono MP3 export from module 2 - it cuts both the upload and your listeners' download.

BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU PROMISE A SPONSOR. Quote the downloads you actually have, from your host's own figures, and never a number you hope for. A sponsor who finds out is not just a lost sponsor, it is a lost reputation in a small market where everyone knows everyone.

AND DECIDE WHETHER YOU WANT A PODCAST OR AN INCOME. They are not the same project, and being honest about which you are pursuing will save you a year.
lessons.practice: Write down which of the five routes is genuinely available to you at your current size, and why the others are not yet. Then, for the route you chose, write the specific first action - the service you would sell, or the local business you would approach - with a name and a date.

quiz.question: Which earning route needs the smallest audience?
options: Selling your own service or product to a small, well-matched audience
Advertising and sponsorship from national brands
Listener donations
Affiliate links

quiz.question: What figures should you quote a prospective sponsor?
options: The downloads you actually have, from your host's own figures
A projection of where you expect to be in six months
The size of your social media following
An industry average for your category

lessons.title: Record and Edit a Podcast Episode
objectives: Take one episode from plan to finished file, end to end
Run a recording session so the edit is short
Finish and publish rather than polish forever
lessons.notes:
THIS IS THE APPLIED PROJECT. Everything in modules 1 to 3 was preparation; here you make one complete episode and put it out.

PLAN BEFORE YOU RECORD. Not a script - a running order. The opening line, three or four things you will cover in order, and how you will end. Ten minutes of this removes an hour of editing, because most editing time is spent cutting the wandering that comes from not knowing what is next.

THE FIRST LINE IS THE WHOLE JOB. A listener decides in about fifteen seconds. Open with the thing itself, not with a welcome, a long introduction, or an apology for not having posted in a while. Record the introduction LAST, once you know what the episode actually turned out to be.

IF YOU HAVE A GUEST: send them the running order beforehand, ask them to sit somewhere soft and quiet, and have them record their own side locally if they possibly can, because a call recording is limited by the worst connection on it. Do a two-minute test with them before the real thing and listen to it. Ask them to keep still and not tap the table.

RECORD IN SECTIONS, not one continuous take. If you fumble, stop, pause, and say the sentence again cleanly - the pause makes it obvious in the waveform and trivial to cut. Trying to push through a mistake is what creates unusable takes and, where power is unreliable, a single long file is also the one most likely to be lost.

EDIT IN ONE PASS AND THEN STOP. Cut the dead air and the mistakes, apply the chain you saved in module 3, normalise, export mono MP3. Resist the urge to listen through a fifth time. A published episode that is ninety per cent right teaches you more than a perfect one still sitting on your laptop, and nobody but you hears the difference.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - finishing and shipping.

WRITE THE EPISODE NOTES AS YOU EDIT, while you still remember what was said: a two-line summary, the names of anyone mentioned, and any link you promised. Doing it later takes three times as long.

NAME AND ARCHIVE THE FILES PROPERLY - date first, then show, then episode number - and keep the raw recording as well as the finished export, in two places. Somebody will eventually ask for a clip from episode three.

DECIDE YOUR SCHEDULE BY WHAT YOU CAN SUSTAIN ON YOUR WORST WEEK, not your best. A fortnightly show that appears reliably beats a weekly one that stops after five episodes, and stopping is what almost all new podcasts do.
lessons.practice: Make one complete episode of ten to fifteen minutes: write a running order, record it in sections in your chosen spot, edit it in a single pass, apply your saved chain, and export it as a mono MP3. Write the episode notes while editing. Then publish it or send it to three people - the point is that it leaves your laptop.

quiz.question: When should the episode introduction be recorded?
options: Last, once you know what the episode actually turned out to be
First, to set the tone before you start
During the edit, using text to speech
It should be the same every week and reused

quiz.question: What should you do when you fumble a sentence mid-recording?
options: Stop, pause, and say it again cleanly - the pause makes the cut obvious and easy
Push through and fix it in the edit
Start the whole recording again
Leave it in, because it sounds natural

lessons.title: Make Your First Voice-Over Demo Reel
objectives: Build a demo that gets listened to past the first ten seconds
Choose the right material for the work you actually want
Avoid the mistakes that make a demo count against you
lessons.notes:
A DEMO IS NOT A SHOWCASE OF EVERYTHING YOU CAN DO. It is a short, targeted answer to one question a producer is asking: can this person do the specific thing I need, today. They will listen for ten or fifteen seconds and then decide.

KEEP IT UNDER NINETY SECONDS, and put your strongest read first. There is no prize for length and nobody reaches the end of a long one.

MAKE SEPARATE DEMOS FOR SEPARATE KINDS OF WORK. A commercial demo, a corporate and e-learning demo, a narration demo. Mixing them tells a producer you are not really any of them. If you make only one, make it the kind of work you actually intend to get.

FIVE TO SEVEN SHORT PIECES, each only ten to fifteen seconds - just enough to establish a tone before moving on. Vary the energy between them so the differences are audible.

WRITE YOUR OWN SCRIPTS OR USE GENUINELY FREE ONES. Do not use a real brand's actual advert, which misrepresents you as having done work you have not, and do not claim credits you do not have. This industry is small and that gets discovered.

NO MUSIC BED UNDERNEATH UNLESS YOU ARE SURE. Beginners hide behind music; producers want to hear the voice. If the demo needs music to sound good, the read is not ready.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO.

YOUR DEMO IS A TECHNICAL SAMPLE AS WELL AS A PERFORMANCE. A producer is also judging whether your recordings will be clean enough to use. A demo with audible room echo or a hiss says the read might be fine but the files will be trouble, and that alone loses jobs. Record the demo in your best spot, on your best day.

MAKE THE DEMO FOR THE MARKET YOU CAN ACTUALLY WIN. A reel of Kenyan English, Swahili and Sheng reads aimed at local radio, phone systems and NGO training is a far stronger opening than an imitation-American commercial reel that competes with thousands. Lead with what makes you the obvious choice rather than a weaker version of someone else.

HOST IT SOMEWHERE THAT OPENS INSTANTLY on a phone, with a direct link and no sign-up between the producer and the audio. Attach it as a small MP3 when asked rather than sending somebody to a site that wants an account.

REDO IT IN SIX MONTHS. Your first demo will embarrass you, which is a sign of progress, not a reason to delay making it now.
lessons.practice: Write five short scripts of about twelve seconds each, in the styles you actually want to be hired for. Record them in your best spot, pick your strongest as the opener, and assemble a demo under ninety seconds with no music. Play it to somebody who does not know you and ask what kind of work they think you do.

quiz.question: How long should a first demo be?
options: Under ninety seconds, with the strongest read first
Three to five minutes, to show range
As long as you have good material for
Exactly one minute per style

quiz.question: Besides the performance, what is a producer judging in a demo?
options: Whether your recordings are technically clean enough to actually use
How many styles you can attempt
Whether you used professional music
How recently it was made

lessons.title: Fiverr Gig Setup for Voice Actors
objectives: Set up a listing that gets found and clicked
Price and package a first offer sensibly
Survive the first few orders, which decide everything
lessons.notes:
ON A MARKETPLACE YOU ARE NOT COMPETING ON TALENT, you are competing on being found and then being chosen in about four seconds. Both are craft, and both are learnable.

BEING FOUND: the title should read like the thing a buyer types, not like a description of you. Something on the pattern of - I will record a warm Kenyan English voice over for your advert - beats anything clever. Use the specific words a buyer would use, including the language and accent, because that is exactly what people search for and it is where you have the least competition.

BEING CHOSEN: the buyer sees a thumbnail and a title. Your sample audio must start with your voice immediately - no music intro, no station-identification flourish. They are clicking through many; you get one chance to be the one that sounds right.

PACKAGING: three tiers, differing in LENGTH and TURNAROUND, not in how hard you try. A basic tier of up to a hundred words in two days, then bigger and faster tiers. Put revisions in writing - two included, further ones charged - because unlimited revisions is how a cheap job eats a week.

PRICING THE FIRST ONE: low enough to get the first orders, and say plainly that it is an introductory rate. The first handful of reviews are worth more than the money, because the listing is invisible without them. Raise the price once you have five.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - what actually decides whether this works.

THE FIRST THREE ORDERS DECIDE THE NEXT THIRTY. Over-deliver on them deliberately: answer within the hour, deliver early, include an extra take at no charge. That behaviour buys reviews, and reviews are the whole economy of the platform.

WORK OUT YOUR REAL NET BEFORE YOU SET A PRICE. The platform takes a commission, the withdrawal route takes a fee, and a currency conversion may take a little more. Do that arithmetic once on paper so you know what a given price actually delivers to you in shillings, and price accordingly instead of being surprised.

BE AVAILABLE WHEN YOUR BUYERS ARE. Response time is measured and it affects how you rank. Kenyan hours cover the European working day and reach the American morning, which is a genuine advantage - and a reason to set expectations honestly rather than promising a two-hour turnaround at three in the morning.

NEVER TAKE A JOB YOU CANNOT DELIVER, and never accept payment or a brief outside the platform while you are building a rating - it removes the protection you are paying commission for, and it is how new sellers get cheated.

FINALLY, THE LISTING IS NOT FINISHED WHEN IT IS PUBLISHED. Change the title, the sample and the thumbnail, and watch what changes. Treat it as something you tune for a month.
lessons.practice: Write a gig title in the exact words a buyer would type, name your three tiers by length and turnaround, and state your revision policy in one sentence. Then do the arithmetic: for a price you are considering, work out what actually reaches you in shillings after commission, withdrawal and conversion. Write that number down.

quiz.question: How should the three tiers of a listing differ?
options: By length and turnaround time, with the revision policy stated in writing
By how much effort you put into the read
By the quality of the microphone used
By how many accents are included

quiz.question: Why over-deliver on the first three orders?
options: The first reviews are what make the listing visible at all - they are worth more than the fee
Early buyers usually pay the most
The platform refunds your commission
It is required before you can raise your price

lessons.title: Finding Clients as a Freelance Podcast Editor
objectives: See why editing is the most reliable income in this field
Find shows that need an editor and approach them well
Price and run the work so it is repeatable
lessons.notes:
PODCAST EDITING IS THE STEADIEST MONEY IN THIS WHOLE COURSE, and it is the least glamorous, which is precisely why there is room in it. Every podcaster starts out editing their own show, every one of them comes to dread it, and the ones whose show survives eventually pay somebody. That somebody can be you, and the work is RECURRING - the same client, every week, indefinitely - which is worth far more than a series of one-off jobs.

YOU ALREADY HAVE THE SKILL. Modules 2 and 3 were the training. Cut the dead air and the mistakes, apply a consistent chain, export to spec, deliver on time. That is the job.

HOW TO FIND THEM: look for shows that are good in content and rough in sound. Inconsistent volume between host and guest, audible room echo, long silences left in, episodes that are late. Those are all signs of somebody editing their own show and struggling. Regional and local shows are the right target - they are reachable, they have no editor, and an international editor is not competing for them.

THE APPROACH THAT WORKS is not an offer, it is a demonstration. Take three minutes of one of their actual episodes, edit it properly, and send both versions with a short note: here is three minutes of episode twelve, cleaned up, it took me twenty minutes, I can do this every week. That converts far better than any pitch, because it removes all the imagining.

PRICE PER EPISODE, NOT PER HOUR. The client wants to know what an episode costs; per-hour pricing also punishes you for getting faster, which you will. Set the price by a typical episode length and a defined scope.

DEFINE THE SCOPE IN WRITING before the first episode: what you cut, what you do not, how many revision rounds, what turnaround, and what happens when they send a three-hour recording instead of the usual one. Scope creep is what turns a good retainer into resentment.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - making it repeatable.

BUILD A TEMPLATE AND A CHECKLIST per client - their chain settings, their intro and outro, their export spec, their file naming. Then every episode is the same twenty minutes of work rather than a fresh decision every time. This is what lets you hold several clients at once, and it is the whole difference between a job and a trade.

HANDLE THE FILE SIZES DELIBERATELY. Raw recordings are large and clients will send them at the worst possible moment on the worst possible connection. Agree a shared folder, ask for compressed uploads where the quality allows, and do your downloading on wifi. Build that reality into your turnaround promise rather than missing deadlines because of it.

GET PAID MONTHLY, IN ADVANCE OR HALF IN ADVANCE, once the relationship is established. Chasing four small invoices a month is a job in itself.

AND KEEP THE RELATIONSHIP, not just the work. The editor who notices that the intro is too long, or that last week's guest was quiet, becomes the person they consult rather than the person they pay - and that one is much harder to replace.
lessons.practice: Find three podcasts with good content and rough audio - regional or local ones you can actually reach. Take three minutes of one real episode, edit it properly, and write the short note you would send with the before and after. Then write your per-episode price and a scope in five lines: what is included, what is not, turnaround, revisions, and what an oversized file costs.

quiz.question: Why is podcast editing the steadiest income in this field?
options: It is recurring - the same client every week - and every podcaster eventually stops wanting to do it
It pays the highest hourly rate
It requires the least skill
Clients pay in advance by default

quiz.question: What is the most effective way to approach a show?
options: Edit three minutes of one of their real episodes and send before and after
Send a list of your equipment and software
Offer the lowest price in the market
Ask them whether they need an editor
